query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A moderate cold deformation process, applied via an 8% cold rolling reduction, will activate work hardening and refine the existing dual-phase lamellar structure of the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic HEA, thereby significantly increasing its strength and creep resistance while maintaining acceptable ductility and corrosion resistance for fastener applications under extreme thermal and mechanical conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with an fcc/B2 dual-phase microstructure, exhibiting a proof stress near 75 MPa, fracture strength approaching 1.2 GPa, and room-temperature ductility of about 22–25%.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to moderate cold rolling with approximately 8% thickness reduction.
generation.conditions: Processing at room temperature with subsequent exposure to extreme temperature fluctuations (up to 700°C), long-term mechanical loading (including room-temperature creep conditions), and corrosive environments relevant to industrial fastener applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The induced increase in dislocation density and subtle refinement of the duplex lamellar (fcc/B2) microstructure, which enhances phase boundary strengthening and impedes dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: Cold rolling introduces work hardening that raises yield and fracture strengths by increasing defect density and refining the lamellar spacing. This refined structure is expected to impede dislocation glide and crack propagation, thereby improving resistance to creep under prolonged loading and serving as barriers to corrosion attack in aggressive environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Enhanced proof and fracture stresses relative to the as-cast state, with strength improvements accompanied by maintained (or only moderately reduced) ductility. In service, the alloy should exhibit improved resistance to room-temperature creep, better performance under thermal fluctuations up to 700°C, and robust corrosion resistance.
generation.baseline: The as-cast, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA with a proof stress of about 75 MPa, a fracture strength near 1.2 GPa (true stress), and elongation of approximately 22–25% at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for eutectic HEAs with similar lamellar architectures under high-temperature exposure (up to ~700°C); further adjustments may be necessary if the operational environment exceeds these limits or if excessive cold work leads to a detrimental loss of ductility.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence supports improvements in strength and a reasonable retention of ductility via moderate cold rolling, the precise balance between work hardening and potential embrittlement, as well as the long-term effects on creep and corrosion resistance under cyclic or aggressive conditions, remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA samples: one in the original as-cast fine lamellar state (control) and one subjected to an 8% cold rolling reduction. Conduct tensile tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (600°C and 700°C) to measure proof stress, fracture strength, and ductility. Additionally, perform room-temperature creep tests and standardized corrosion tests in an aggressive medium. Compare the mechanical and environmental performance of both sets.
measurements: Creep rate (strain rate under constant load)
Corrosion rate (mass loss or electrochemical metrics)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cold-rolled samples do not show statistically significant increases in yield and fracture strength, or if their ductility falls below an acceptable industrial threshold (e.g., a dramatic drop in elongation), and if they display similar or worsened creep or corrosion behavior compared with the control, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5).
